draft.title: Life on the manor
card: A manor was a lord's estate. It included his house, farmland, pasture and a village. Most people in medieval Europe were peasants who lived and worked on a manor.
a peasant who was bound to the land. A serf could not leave the manor without the lord's permission.
Serfs worked the lord's fields for a set number of days each week. They also farmed their own strips of land to feed their families.
In return for using the land and for the lord's protection, serfs paid him part of their crops. They were not paid wages for the work they did on his fields.
draft.remember: A manor ran on peasant labour: serfs were tied to the land and owed the lord work and a share of their crops.

a.q: Which of these best describes a serf on a medieval manor?
opts: A peasant tied to the land who worked for the lord
A peasant who was free to move to any town
A knight who was given a manor by the king
A craftsman who was paid wages by the lord
a.why: A serf was bound to the manor and owed the lord work and part of the crops. A knight held land for fighting, not as a serf, and serfs were not paid wages for working the lord's fields.
a.clue: Think about whether a serf could leave.

b.q: Tom is a serf on a manor in England. Which of these would he most likely have done?
opts: Worked the lord's fields and gave him part of his crops
Left the manor to find better paid work in another county
Sold his crops and kept all the money for himself
Collected rent from other peasants on the manor
b.why: Serfs worked the lord's fields and paid him part of their crops. Tom could not simply leave the manor, so moving for better paid work is the tempting but wrong choice.
b.clue: A serf owed the lord both work and a share of what he grew.

a.best: A peasant tied to the land who worked for the lord

b.best: Worked the lord's fields and gave him part of his crops

problems.detail: The clue ('A serf owed the lord both work and a share of what he grew') almost repeats the right option, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea. A clue that points to the idea without matching the option's wording would work better.
